content: The recommended antiretroviral regimens for treatment include the following options: Tipranavir (TPV) at a dose of 200 mg twice daily, or a combination of Lopinavir (LPV) 400 mg and Ritonavir (RTV) 400 mg twice daily, or Saquinavir (SQV) 400 mg with Ritonavir (RTV) 400 mg twice daily. Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs), such as Raltegravir (RAL) at 400 mg twice daily, are also recommended. For adolescents weighing less than 35 kg, weight-based dosing guidelines for antiretroviral formulations should be consulted. Annex 7 of the guidelines provides detailed information on weight-based dosing for antiretroviral drugs in children. This includes prescribing information and dosing recommendations for infants and children based on available evidence and pediatric indications. The World Health Organization (WHO), through the Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group, has developed simplified guidance to facilitate the use of antiretroviral drugs in children. Doses are expressed per weight band rather than per kilogram or body surface area to simplify implementation. The weight-band dosing approach considers the typical body surface area of children in lowand middle-income countries. The primary source of dosing information is the manufacturer’s package insert, supplemented by clinical studies and expert consultations in pediatric pharmacology. In some cases, the dose for a specific weight band may slightly exceed or fall below the manufacturer’s recommended target dose due to limitations of fixed-dose combinations. Antiretroviral drugs that are no longer considered preferred or alternative options for children, such as Didanosine and Saquinavir, have been excluded from the dosing guidance. The Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group has emphasized the need for further data before recommending Efavirenz (EFV) for children under three years of age. The simplified dosing schedule will be regularly reviewed and updated as new data or formulations become available. National programs are advised to refer to the most recent product labeling for up-to-date information. The guidelines recommend using age-appropriate fixed-dose combinations whenever available. Oral liquid or syrup formulations should be avoided if large volumes are required (e.g., over 10 mL). Dispersible tablets are preferred as they can be converted into liquid at the point of use. Young children should transition to solid oral dosage forms as soon as they can tolerate them. When adult formulations are used for children, care must be taken to avoid underdosing. Scored adult tablets are easier to split, but for tablets that are not easily divided, pharmacies should use appropriate tablet cutters. Certain formulations, such as heat-stable Lopinavir/Ritonavir (LPV/r) tablets, should not be split or crushed as this compromises bioavailability. Children must be weighed at every clinic visit, and doses should be adjusted as they grow or gain weight. Simplified dosing tables for child-friendly solid formulations and oral liquids are provided for both once-daily and twice-daily regimens. For example, Nevirapine (NVP) dose escalation with a half-dose for two weeks is recommended when initiating antiretroviral therapy to minimize toxicity. However, recent data suggest that younger children may have a lower risk of toxicity, and starting with a full dose may be considered in some cases. The Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group has highlighted the urgent need for new formulations, particularly fixed-dose combinations containing LPV/r in solid forms suitable for young children, scored Tenofovir (TDF) tablets, and TDF-based fixed-dose combinations for children. Heat-stable formulations of Atazanavir/Ritonavir (ATV/r) and Darunavir/Ritonavir (DRV/r) are also critical for treatment sequencing. Access to a heat-stable formulation containing 30 mg of Ritonavir is important for super-boosting Lopinavir in the context of rifampicin-based tuberculosis treatment. The recent approval of Efavirenz (EFV) for children aged three months to three years provides an additional treatment option and an opportunity for harmonization across age groups. As more data become available, sprinkle formulations of EFV should be made accessible in resource-limited settings. WHO continues to work with pharmaceutical partners to simplify prescribing, dispensing, and dosing guidance and to develop practical recommendations for scaling up antiretroviral therapy for children. While the listing of a formulation in the annex does not guarantee quality assurance, it is essential to verify that the product meets regulatory standards.
